title: Seismology of Glasses
comment: 7 pages, 2 figures. Any comments or suggestions are welcome!
summary: Aging and relaxation of glasses proceed through localized rearrangements that also generate long-ranged mechanical responses in their surroundings. We develop a theory that treats these rearrangements as internal microseismic sources, and thereby separates the direct effects emerging from an event from the effects from the far-field displacements it generates. These far-field disturbances propagate and relax through the viscoelastic medium through which they move, producing a stochastic background of weak but numerous perturbations at any given location. Combining the description of local events from the Random First Order Transition theory with this propagating background, we derive a unified equation for the dynamical structure factor of a relaxing glass. The theory identifies a finite wave-vector and time window in which the growing viscoelastic far-field disturbances can produce compressed exponential relaxation, which has been observed using X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy. At higher wave vectors that resolve local jumps, heterogeneity of the local event dynamics instead produces stretched exponential relaxation. The crossover between these behaviors depends on the event statistics and the scattering phase accumulated across the region reached through viscoelastic propagation from the numerous distant sources.

AI.tldr: A theory treating local aging rearrangements in glasses as microseismic sources separates direct event effects from propagating far-field disturbances; combining RFOT local-event statistics with the viscoelastic background yields a unified dynamical structure factor predicting compressed exponential relaxation at intermediate wave vectors and stretched exponential relaxation at high wave vectors.
AI.motivation: Aging and relaxation in glasses arise from localized rearrangements that also emit long-ranged mechanical responses, but existing treatments do not clearly disentangle the direct effect of an event from the far-field displacements it generates and propagates through the viscoelastic medium. The paper aims to explain why XPCS observes compressed exponential relaxation at certain length and time scales while local-jump-resolving scales show stretched exponential behavior.
AI.method: Localized rearrangements are modeled as internal microseismic sources. The direct near-event contribution is separated from far-field displacements, which propagate and relax through the viscoelastic medium and accumulate as a stochastic background at any location. Local event statistics from Random First Order Transition (RFOT) theory are combined with this propagating background to derive a unified equation for the dynamical structure factor of a relaxing glass.
AI.result: The theory identifies a finite wave-vector and time window in which growing viscoelastic far-field disturbances generate compressed exponential relaxation, matching XPCS observations. At higher wave vectors that resolve local jumps, heterogeneity of local event dynamics instead produces stretched exponential relaxation. The crossover between these regimes is controlled by the event statistics and the scattering phase accumulated across the region reached by viscoelastic propagation from numerous distant sources.
AI.conclusion: The far-field microseismic background from localized rearrangements, rather than local events alone, drives compressed exponential relaxation in glasses. A single unified dynamical structure factor reproduces both compressed and stretched exponential regimes observed in XPCS, with the crossover governed by event statistics and accumulated propagation phase.

title: Resolving Structural Uncertainty in Stochastic Dynamical Systems via Ensemble-Based Bayesian Inference
comment: 14 pages article, 4 figures article, 5 pages SM, 1 figure SM
summary: Recovering the interaction structure of complex stochastic dynamical systems from sparse time-series observations is an inherently ill-posed inverse problem. The posterior over network configurations is high-dimensional, highly degenerate, and shaped by the non-equilibrium nature of the available data. To address this, we propose a fully Bayesian, ensemble-based inference framework. Our approach grounds a continuous-time Stochastic Differential Equation (SDE) likelihood formulation---acting mathematically as an Onsager-Machlup quasi-potential for non-equilibrium paths---within a non-parametric Minimum Description Length (MDL) structural prior. This framework rigorously penalizes model complexity and avoids kinetic overfitting by forcing continuous parameters into a finite vocabulary of discrete categories. The joint posterior is optimized using a block-coordinate scheme combining sub-quadratic Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) topological sampling with deterministic Nelder-Mead parameter optimization. Using highly non-linear macroscopic population dynamics as a benchmark, we demonstrate that inference requires non-stationary transient data to resolve causal information. Furthermore, we prove that propagating structural uncertainty via ensemble-based posterior analysis produces significantly more robust and reliable predictions for downstream perturbation outcomes than traditional single-point (MAP) estimates. The framework is highly generalizable, capturing fundamental topological constraints even under severe generative model mismatches, offering a robust tool for uncertainty-aware inference in complex stochastic systems.

AI.tldr: A fully Bayesian, ensemble-based framework recovers interaction structure of complex stochastic dynamical systems from sparse time series by combining an SDE likelihood (Onsager-Machlup quasi-potential) with a non-parametric MDL prior, optimized via block-coordinate MCMC and Nelder-Mead.
AI.motivation: Recovering interaction structure of complex stochastic dynamical systems from sparse time-series is inherently ill-posed: the posterior over network configurations is high-dimensional, highly degenerate, and shaped by non-equilibrium data. Existing methods risk kinetic overfitting and provide only single-point estimates lacking structural uncertainty.
AI.method: A fully Bayesian, ensemble-based inference framework. It grounds a continuous-time SDE likelihood acting as an Onsager-Machlup quasi-potential for non-equilibrium paths within a non-parametric Minimum Description Length structural prior. Continuous parameters are forced into a finite vocabulary of discrete categories to penalize complexity and avoid kinetic overfitting. The joint posterior is optimized with a block-coordinate scheme combining sub-quadratic MCMC topological sampling and deterministic Nelder-Mead parameter optimization.
AI.result: Benchmarked on highly non-linear macroscopic population dynamics: inference requires non-stationary transient data to resolve causal information. Ensemble-based posterior analysis propagating structural uncertainty yields significantly more robust and reliable predictions of downstream perturbation outcomes than traditional single-point (MAP) estimates. The framework captures fundamental topological constraints even under severe generative model mismatches.
AI.conclusion: The framework is highly generalizable and offers a robust tool for uncertainty-aware inference in complex stochastic systems, demonstrating the value of ensemble-based structural uncertainty propagation over point estimates.

title: Deep Learning of Phase Transitions for Bilinear-Biquadratic Spin-1 Chains from Correlation Aspects
summary: We investigate the role of different correlation functions in reconstructing the phase diagram of the spin-1 bilinear-biquadratic chain, parametrized by the angle $θ$ between the bilinear and biquadratic couplings, using our previously developed label-free machine-learning pipeline \cite{Ming21, Ming23}, in which an autoencoder compresses iDMRG correlation matrices into latent features and K-means clustering with silhouette analysis groups them into phases. Without any prior labels, the scheme reveals four natural phases, the Haldane, dimerized, critical trimerized, and ferromagnetic phases, and accurately locates the Takhtajan-Babujian ($θ=-π/4$), $SU(3)$-symmetric Uimin-Lai-Sutherland ($θ=π/4$), and Ferro-Dimer ($θ=5π/4$) transition points; a shallow supervised refinement further sharpens the phase boundaries. We find that different correlation functions play fundamentally different roles in phase identification. The $SU(3)$-symmetric correlation alone selects a four-cluster partition that can be associated with the four phases, whereas the spin-spin and dimer-dimer correlations must be combined to recover the complete phase diagram. In contrast, the trimer-trimer correlation behaves as a marginal correlation: it is insufficient for phase identification by itself but improves the precision of the predicted phase boundaries when combined with the other correlations. Furthermore, the latent representations and silhouette values reveal signatures that we relate to the $θ$ dependence of the correlations within each phase and, tentatively, to the underlying renormalization-group structure. These results demonstrate that machine learning can not only identify quantum phases but also uncover the physical information encoded in different correlation functions.

AI.tldr: A label-free machine-learning pipeline (autoencoder + K-means/silhouette) reconstructs the spin-1 bilinear-biquadratic chain phase diagram, revealing four phases and locating three transition points; different correlation functions play distinct roles, with SU(3) correlation alone sufficient for four-phase identification, spin-spin + dimer-dimer needed for the full diagram, and trimer-trimer acting as a marginal, boundary-sharpening correlation.
AI.motivation: The paper probes the role of different correlation functions in phase reconstruction of the spin-1 bilinear-biquadratic chain. The goal is to determine which correlation functions are necessary or sufficient for identifying quantum phases, and to show that machine learning can uncover physical information encoded in different correlations beyond mere phase labeling.
AI.method: An autoencoder compresses iDMRG correlation matrices into latent features; K-means clustering with silhouette analysis groups them into phases without any prior labels. A shallow supervised refinement sharpens phase boundaries. Correlation functions examined: SU(3)-symmetric, spin-spin, dimer-dimer, and trimer-trimer correlations.
AI.result: The scheme reveals four natural phases without labels: Haldane, dimerized, critical trimerized, and ferromagnetic. It accurately locates the Takhtajan-Babujian (θ=-π/4), SU(3)-symmetric Uimin-Lai-Sutherland (θ=π/4), and Ferro-Dimer (θ=5π/4) transition points. The SU(3)-symmetric correlation alone selects a four-cluster partition matching the four phases; spin-spin and dimer-dimer correlations must be combined to recover the complete phase diagram; trimer-trimer correlation is marginal—insufficient alone but improves boundary precision when combined.
AI.conclusion: Latent representations and silhouette values reveal signatures related to the θ dependence of correlations within each phase and, tentatively, to the underlying renormalization-group structure. Machine learning can not only identify quantum phases but also uncover the physical information encoded in different correlation functions, with different correlation functions playing fundamentally different roles in phase identification.

title: Testing Replica Symmetry Breaking in the three-dimensional Edwards-Anderson model by using vanishing fields
summary:
Replica Symmetry Breaking (RSB) theory for spin glasses, which is exact in infinite dimensions, provides detailed predictions for the behavior of these systems. One of these predictions is that vanishing magnetic fields induce chaotic behavior. Here, vanishing has a precise meaning: we refer to an externally applied magnetic field with intensity scaling as $1/\sqrt{N}$, where $N$ is the number of spins in the system. RSB predicts that this chaotic behavior depends only on the probability density function of the overlap, $P(q)$, as computed at zero field.
  We proceed to test the RSB prediction in the 3D Edwards-Anderson model, by first computing the $P(q)$ numerically in the absence of a magnetic field. We then use this function as input to analytically compute the statistics of the states in the regime of a vanishing magnetic field, using a representation based on the Bolthausen-Sznitman coalescent process (which is exact for the mean-field Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model). This mixed numerical-analytical approach allows us to determine the prediction of RSB for the overlap distribution function measured in the presence of a small vanishing field, as well as the increase in chaoticity as the field strength grows.
  The above RSB predictions are quantitatively compared with the outcome of numerical simulations of the three-dimensional Edwards-Anderson in the presence of a small vanishing field, finding very good agreement. This agreement provides strong support for the idea that three-dimensional spin glass at zero magnetic field and low temperature is well described by RSB theory.

AI.tldr: The paper tests Replica Symmetry Breaking (RSB) theory in the 3D Edwards-Anderson spin glass by combining numerical computation of the zero-field overlap distribution P(q) with an analytical coalescent-based method to predict behavior under vanishing magnetic fields, finding strong quantitative agreement with simulations.
AI.motivation: RSB theory, exact in infinite dimensions, predicts that vanishing magnetic fields (intensity scaling as 1/sqrt(N)) induce chaotic behavior depending only on the zero-field overlap distribution P(q). Testing this prediction in a finite-dimensional (3D) system is important to assess whether RSB theory correctly describes 3D spin glasses at low temperature and zero field.
AI.method: A mixed numerical-analytical approach: first numerically compute P(q) in the 3D Edwards-Anderson model at zero field, then use this P(q) as input to analytically compute the state statistics in the vanishing-field regime via a representation based on the Bolthausen-Sznitman coalescent process (exact for the mean-field Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model). This yields RSB predictions for the overlap distribution function under a small vanishing field and for the increase in chaoticity with field strength.
AI.result: RSB predictions were quantitatively compared with numerical simulations of the 3D Edwards-Anderson model in a small vanishing field, showing very good agreement.
AI.conclusion: The agreement provides strong support for the idea that the 3D spin glass at zero magnetic field and low temperature is well described by RSB theory.

title: Optimal Disorder Strength for Approximate Unitary $k$-Designs in Spin Chains
comment: main text: 5 pages, 3 figures. Supplementary material 9 pages, 3 figures
summary: Quantum simulators with disordered spin Hamiltonians offer a natural route to Haar-like unitary ensembles, but face a competition. Disorder enhances randomness, yet strong disorder suppresses dynamics and localizes the system in the computational basis. This suggests an optimal intermediate disorder strength for approximating a unitary $k$-design, which has so far been identified mainly empirically. Here, we develop a perturbative theory for the moment gap $Δ^{(k)}$, the deviation of the $k$-th moment operator from its Haar value, for the full spectrum of the interacting XXZ chain in a fixed-magnetization sector. We find the non-monotonic asymptotic scalings $\ln Δ^{(k)}\sim -σ^2$ at weak disorder and $\ln Δ^{(k)}\sim -1/σ$ at strong disorder, whose crossover sets an optimal disorder strength $σ_c\sim J_{xy}$, where $J_{xy}$ is the energy scale of the non-random interaction. We further show that a multi-quench protocol further suppresses the gap exponentially in the number of quenches. Numerical simulations confirm both scalings and this exponential suppression, and we demonstrate the usefulness of the protocol for classical shadow tomography. This work suggests that strong disorder may block both thermalization and the formation of unitary designs through a common localization mechanism.

AI.tldr: A perturbative theory for the moment gap Δ^(k) of the interacting XXZ chain in a fixed-magnetization sector reveals non-monotonic scaling (ln Δ^(k) ~ -σ² at weak disorder, ~ -1/σ at strong disorder), with an optimal disorder strength σ_c ~ J_{xy}, and a multi-quench protocol that exponentially suppresses the gap.
AI.motivation: Disordered spin Hamiltonians are a natural way to realize Haar-like unitary k-designs, but disorder plays a double-edged role: it enhances randomness while strong disorder localizes the system and suppresses dynamics. This tradeoff implies an optimal intermediate disorder strength, which until now has been identified mainly empirically rather than from theory.
AI.method: The authors develop a perturbative theory for the moment gap Δ^(k) — the deviation of the k-th moment operator from its Haar value — covering the full spectrum of the interacting XXZ chain in a fixed-magnetization sector. They analyze the asymptotic scaling of Δ^(k) in both the weak- and strong-disorder regimes, characterize the crossover, and introduce a multi-quench protocol whose suppression of the gap is verified via numerical simulations.
AI.result: The theory yields non-monotonic asymptotic scalings: ln Δ^(k) ~ -σ² at weak disorder and ln Δ^(k) ~ -1/σ at strong disorder, with a crossover setting an optimal disorder strength σ_c ~ J_{xy}, where J_{xy} is the energy scale of the non-random interaction. A multi-quench protocol further suppresses the gap exponentially in the number of quenches. Numerical simulations confirm both scalings and the exponential suppression, and the protocol is shown to be useful for classical shadow tomography.
AI.conclusion: Strong disorder may block both thermalization and the formation of unitary designs through a common localization mechanism. The results provide a theoretical basis for choosing disorder strength and quench protocols to approximate unitary k-designs.
